description: Where new business owners go for help — finance, professional, community and government support.
content_html:
Why Do New Business Owners Need Support?

Starting a business is rarely a solo journey. Most new entrepreneurs encounter questions they cannot answer alone — how to manage accounts, whether a contract is legally sound, how to apply for funding, or how to find other local businesses to learn from. Knowing where to find the right help, at the right moment, can be the difference between a business that survives its first year and one that fails through avoidable mistakes.

The kind of support a start-up needs changes at different stages. In the early days, the focus is often on finance and legal structure. Later, it might be about finding customers or managing staff. The key skill — and what this lesson explores — is matching the right type of support to the right problem.

Sources of Support

There are several different categories of support available to a new business. Some provide money, some provide expertise, some provide community and connections, and some provide practical services. A smart entrepreneur draws on more than one.

A bank can provide a range of financial products to a new business: loans to fund start-up costs, business current accounts for day-to-day transactions, and access to financial advice. Banks typically want evidence that the business has a credible plan and a realistic chance of repaying any money borrowed. For a brand-new business with no trading history, getting finance from a bank can be challenging — which is why many entrepreneurs combine bank support with other sources.

A business angel is a private investor who provides capital in exchange for a share of the business and often a seat at the table as a mentor or advisor. Beyond the money itself, a business angel typically brings industry experience, a network of useful contacts, and a genuine stake in seeing the business succeed. This can be especially valuable for a start-up whose founder has a great idea but limited business experience.

The government provides a range of support for new businesses through national schemes and programmes. This can include grants (money that does not need to be repaid), information and guidance on starting up, and training or mentoring schemes. Government support is typically targeted at specific types of business, industries or locations, so a new enterprise must check whether it qualifies before applying.

A local council enterprise department often offers support that is specifically tailored to businesses in that area. This might include help with finding suitable premises, advice on local business rates, introductions to other local businesses, and information about area-specific grants or regeneration funding. Local support tends to be more accessible for a brand-new small business than national programmes, which may be more competitive.

An accountant helps a new business keep on top of its finances. For a start-up, this typically includes setting up bookkeeping systems, preparing tax returns, making sure the business meets its legal obligations to report income, and advising on whether the business is generating profit or heading towards difficulty. Many sole traders and small partnerships use an accountant even if they could manage some of these tasks themselves, simply because professional financial management reduces costly errors.

A solicitor is a legal expert. A new business may need a solicitor to draft or review contracts, register a trademark, advise on the legal structure of a partnership or company, or handle any dispute with a supplier or customer. Legal mistakes are often expensive — a poorly written contract, for example, could leave the business without recourse if a major customer refuses to pay. Using a solicitor early to set up the right legal foundations is often cheaper than dealing with problems later.

Friends and family can be a source of informal support that goes well beyond money. A family member with marketing experience might help with social media. A friend who has set up their own business might share practical advice about what worked and what did not. This informal network is often the first port of call for a new entrepreneur and should not be underestimated.

The Chamber of Commerce is a membership organisation for local businesses. Joining gives access to networking events where entrepreneurs can meet potential customers, suppliers and partners. The Chamber often provides training sessions, business advice workshops and a collective voice to advocate for local business interests to the council or government. For a new start-up looking to build its local network quickly, the Chamber of Commerce can be a genuinely practical resource.

Charitable organisations exist in most parts of the UK to support new or struggling businesses, particularly those run by people from disadvantaged backgrounds or those operating in areas of economic need. Charitable support might include free or subsidised business mentoring, access to shared workspace, help with writing a business plan, or connections to grant funding. Unlike banks, charities are not looking for a financial return, so the support they provide is often more accessible for an early-stage business that has not yet proven its viability.

Key Fact

Eight sources of support for a new enterprise: bank (loans, accounts, financial advice), business angel (capital plus mentoring and contacts), government (grants and guidance schemes), local council enterprise department (local premises, rates and area-specific funding), accountant (financial management and tax), solicitor (contracts and legal structure), friends and family (informal advice and support), Chamber of Commerce (networking and training), charities (mentoring and accessible support for early-stage businesses).

Choosing the Right Support

The analytical skill that examiners reward is not just listing sources of support — it is matching the right support to the right situation. Consider three different entrepreneurs:

  • Kezia is starting a food business but has no experience of bookkeeping or tax returns. An accountant is the most directly useful professional for her at this stage, before mistakes accumulate.
  • Marcus is a young entrepreneur with a strong product idea but no industry contacts and limited business experience. A business angel would provide both capital and the mentoring he needs to avoid common pitfalls — at the cost of giving up some ownership.
  • Priya wants to rent a workshop in her town and is looking for local grants. A local council enterprise department is the most targeted starting point, since they hold information about local premises and area-specific funding that national sources would not know about.

In each case, the most appropriate source of support depends on the specific challenge the entrepreneur is facing. A high-mark answer in an exam will always connect the type of support to the entrepreneur’s situation explicitly.

The R067 spec assesses your ability to match support to a specific situation. Identify the entrepreneur's biggest current problem first (cash, legal, premises, expertise), then pick the support source that solves that exact problem.
exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark Explain question on sources of support, the common mistake is listing lots of sources without explaining why any of them suit the business in the question. Pick one or two sources and build a reason chain: what this source provides — why that is relevant to the specific entrepreneur’s challenge — what the consequence is for the business. For a 6-mark Analyse question, develop at least two well-connected points that each link a specific source of support to the business context. Generic answers that could describe any start-up stall in the Developing tier. Examiner reports consistently identify application to the scenario as the key discriminator on medium and extended-mark questions — use the business name, the product, the location or the owner’s background to embed your analysis.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sources of support for a new enterprise include finance providers (bank, business angel), government and local council, professional advisors (accountant, solicitor), community and network support (friends, family, Chamber of Commerce) and charitable organisations.
  • Different sources suit different situations: banks and business angels help with capital; accountants and solicitors prevent costly legal and financial errors; local councils and charities offer accessible support for early-stage businesses.
  • In exam questions, the skill is matching the right support to the specific entrepreneur’s challenge — always link your answer to the details of the scenario rather than listing all support sources.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the role of a Chamber of Commerce?
A) A government body that issues grants directly to new businesses
B) A membership organisation that supports local businesses through networking and training
C) A bank that provides loans and financial advice to small start-ups
D) A legal firm that drafts contracts for new businesses
practice_questions.marks: B) A membership organisation that supports local businesses through networking and training [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which an accountant can support a new start-up business.
practice_questions.marks:
Accept any one of the following (1 mark for one correct answer on a 1-mark State question):
• Setting up bookkeeping systems to track income and expenses
• Preparing tax returns and ensuring the business meets its legal tax obligations
• Advising on whether the business is generating profit
• Helping manage payroll for any employees
[1 mark for any one correctly stated function of an accountant]

practice_questions.text: Describe one way a local council enterprise department can support a new business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for a valid way and 1 mark for development:
• A local council enterprise department can help a new business find suitable premises in the area (1 mark) by providing information about available commercial spaces and local business rates, which reduces the time and cost the entrepreneur would spend searching independently (1 mark).
[Accept any valid function — local grants, local networking introductions, business rates advice — with a brief development of why it helps]

practice_questions.text:
Tansy is a recent graduate who has just launched a sustainable clothing brand from her home in Leicester. She has a strong product but no industry contacts, very limited business experience, and she needs funding to order her first large batch of stock.

Explain why a business angel might be a more suitable source of support for Tansy than a bank loan.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for a developed reason chain:
• A business angel provides capital like a bank loan but also offers mentoring and industry contacts (1 mark), which is particularly valuable for Tansy because her main weakness is limited business experience and no contacts in the fashion industry (1 mark). A bank would provide the funding but would not offer the guidance Tansy needs to avoid common start-up mistakes (1 mark), meaning the business angel addresses both of Tansy's gaps simultaneously, though at the cost of giving up a share of ownership (1 mark).
[1 mark for identifying that a business angel offers more than money; 1 mark for linking the mentoring/contacts to Tansy's specific situation; 1 mark for contrast with a bank's limitations; 1 mark for awareness of the trade-off (loss of ownership)]

practice_questions.text:
Coppice Brew Co. is a new craft beer brand founded by two friends, Eli and Nadia, in a rural part of Wales. They have a product they are proud of, a small amount of personal savings, and limited knowledge of financial management or legal contracts. They are also struggling to find customers beyond their local village.

Analyse two sources of support that would be most appropriate for Coppice Brew Co. at this stage.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two sources of support are identified and each is analytically developed, connecting the specific benefits of that support to the specific challenges Coppice Brew Co. faces (limited finance, no financial management knowledge, no legal experience, limited customer reach). Contextual details (rural Wales, craft beer, two founders) are embedded rather than added as a label. The response shows awareness of why each source is more appropriate than alternatives.

Secure (3-4 marks): Two sources are identified with some development and at least one contextual link. The response shows understanding of what each source provides and why it is relevant.

Developing (2 marks): One or two sources are named with limited analytical development. The link to the specific business is weak or absent.

Emerging (1 mark): One source is named with little or no development.

practice_questions.text:
Iris is planning to open a children's art studio in a market town. She has found a good premises but is unsure whether to use a solicitor to draft her lease agreement or to sign the landlord's standard contract without legal advice, saving approximately £500.

Justify whether Iris should use a solicitor to review her lease agreement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A clear recommendation is made and justified with developed reasoning linked to the specific context (art studio, market town premises, lease agreement, £500 saving). The student builds a reason chain explaining the risk of not using a solicitor and why that risk outweighs the cost, or develops a credible alternative if recommending against. The conclusion adds a new evaluative point rather than restating earlier arguments.

Secure (3-4 marks): A recommendation is made with clear reasoning and some contextual reference. At least one developed point about the risk or benefit of using a solicitor.

Developing (2 marks): A preference is stated with some reasoning but the analysis is general. Context is used superficially.

Emerging (1 mark): A preference is stated with limited or no reasoning.

knowledge_checks.q: Which source of support provides capital AND mentoring and industry contacts in exchange for a share of the business?
What is the primary role of a solicitor for a new business?
options: Managing the business's bookkeeping and tax returns
Providing loans at competitive interest rates
Advising on legal matters such as contracts and business structure
Offering networking events and training workshops

knowledge_checks.q: A membership organisation that supports local businesses through networking events, training and advocacy is called a _____ of Commerce.
A qualified financial professional who helps a business manage accounts, payroll and tax obligations is called an _____.
Match each source of support to the specific help it provides:
right: Loans, business accounts and financial advice for day-to-day operations
Financial management, tax returns and bookkeeping
Information on local premises, business rates and area-specific funding

flashcard_questions.q: What type of support can a bank provide to a new start-up?
flashcard_questions.a: Loans, business current accounts and financial advice.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a business angel offer beyond financial investment?
flashcard_questions.a: Mentoring, industry experience and a network of contacts.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a business angel receive in return for investing?
flashcard_questions.a: A share of the business and often an advisory or mentoring role.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an accountant's main role for a new start-up?
flashcard_questions.a: Managing finances, preparing tax returns and ensuring legal reporting obligations are met.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a solicitor's main role for a new start-up?
flashcard_questions.a: Advising on legal matters such as contracts, business structure and intellectual property.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Chamber of Commerce?
flashcard_questions.a: A membership organisation that supports local businesses in an area.

flashcard_questions.q: How can friends and family provide support beyond money?
flashcard_questions.a: Through informal advice, practical skills and sharing experience from their own careers or businesses.

flashcard_questions.q: What makes charitable support particularly accessible for an early-stage business?
flashcard_questions.a: Charities do not require proof of financial viability or expect a financial return.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a local council enterprise department typically help a new business with?
flashcard_questions.a: Finding local premises, understanding business rates and accessing area-specific grants.

flashcard_questions.q: In an exam question on support, what must you always do to reach the higher mark bands?
flashcard_questions.a: Link the support type to the specific problem the entrepreneur in the scenario faces.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between government grants and bank loans?
flashcard_questions.a: Grants do not need to be repaid; bank loans must be repaid with interest.

glossary_terms.definition: Guidance, resources or connections provided to a new business owner to help it start, grow or overcome a specific problem.
A qualified financial professional who helps a business manage its accounts, tax obligations, payroll and financial reporting.
A qualified legal professional who advises a business on contracts, employment law, intellectual property and other legal obligations.
A membership organisation that supports local businesses through networking events, advocacy, training and shared resources.
